title: Where did all the sitcoms go?

segments: Sitcoms like Seinfeld, The Office, and How I Met Your Mother are no longer being made as much as they used to be. These shows were popular because they had a long tail of success, meaning they continued to be watched and sold for years after they ended.
In the 1990s, sitcoms made up about 12% of new shows. In the 2020s, that number is less than 2%. Even though sitcoms are still popular, many of them ended their runs over a decade ago.

Mike Schur, a sitcom creator, says the economics of TV changed with the rise of streaming. In the past, sitcoms could lose money on their first run but make money later through syndication, where reruns are sold to other channels.

Streaming changed this model. Now, streamers buy shows for fewer episodes, which increases production costs. This is because of an accounting principle called amortization, where the cost of a big purchase is spread out over time. Fewer episodes mean the cost per episode is higher.

Another challenge for sitcoms is that they often need time to develop. They need several episodes to find their rhythm, but streaming platforms want shows that can attract viewers quickly. This makes it hard for sitcoms to experiment and find their footing.
Streaming platforms also measure success differently. They count minutes watched, not the number of households tuning in. This makes hour-long shows more valuable than half-hour sitcoms.

Because of these changes, sitcoms are less valuable overseas and more expensive to make. This has led streamers to focus more on other types of shows, like dramas, which are easier to sell internationally.

Mike Schur is trying to adapt to the new model. His new show, Dig, has elements of workplace comedy and cliffhangers to keep viewers watching. It's tailored to the current era and includes a central mystery to drive engagement.

Mike says it's hard to convince streamers to make traditional sitcoms with long seasons and casual, hangout-style storytelling. He doesn't know of anyone who has successfully done this in the streaming era.
summary.headline: Why are sitcoms becoming less common in the streaming era?
summary.tldr: Sitcoms are becoming less common because streaming changed the economics of TV. Sitcoms are harder to make profitable now, and they need more time to develop, which streaming platforms don't always allow.

key_points.point: Sitcoms used to be profitable through syndication, but streaming has changed that model.
key_points.why_it_matters: This has made sitcoms more expensive to produce and less valuable to streamers.

key_points.point: Streaming platforms measure success by minutes watched, not by the number of households tuning in.

key_points.point: Sitcoms are harder to sell internationally because humor is cultural and doesn't always translate.

summary.lesson: The way we make and watch TV has changed, and sitcoms are struggling to adapt. Understanding these changes can help explain why certain types of shows are more common now than others.
opinions_and_predictions: Mike Schur says that the economics of streaming have made it harder to make traditional sitcoms. He believes that the system doesn't give comedies the time they need to develop.
